title: Julian of Norwich (c. 1343–after 1416)
hook: a woman walled in beside a church sees that all shall be well

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement, the pope who named the lie behind the killings. Your line was no scapegoats. Did you catch the room looking for someone to blame? Day eight hundred twenty-two.

Against the wall of a church in Norwich, in England, stands a small room. One window looks into the church, toward the altar, so the woman inside can follow the Mass. Another opens to the outside, so people from the town can come and talk to her. She does not come out. She has chosen this, with the Church's blessing, and she will spend her life here, praying. Her own name isn't certain. We know her by the name of the church, Saint Julian's. Today's word is the life she chose: anchoress.
screen: `A ROOM AGAINST A CHURCH WALL.` → `ONE WINDOW IN, ONE WINDOW OUT.` → `WE KNOW HER AS JULIAN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. An anchoress is a woman who, with the bishop's blessing, is enclosed for life in a cell attached to a church, to give her days to prayer. A man who did the same was called an anchorite. It sounds like a prison, but it was a vocation, asked for and tested, and people from the town could come to the window for counsel. Next, the showings. Julian writes that she once fell so sick that those around her thought she was dying. A priest held a crucifix before her eyes. Then, she says, she was given a series of showings, visions of Christ's passion and of God's love, and she spent years thinking about them and writing them down. The book is called Revelations of Divine Love. Then, the line. Julian lived in the same century as the plague we met yesterday, and she does not look away from sin or pain. She asks, plainly, why God allowed sin at all. The answer she hears, in Grace Warrack's translation, is this: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Finally, what the line is not. It isn't a shrug, and it isn't a promise that nothing bad will happen. Julian hears it in the middle of her question about sin and suffering, and she keeps asking afterward. It's a promise spoken from inside the pain, about where things are going, not a denial of where they are.
screen: `ENCLOSED BESIDE A CHURCH, FOR LIFE.` · `SICK, AND SHOWN A CRUCIFIX.` · `WHY DID GOD ALLOW SIN?` · `A PROMISE FROM INSIDE THE PAIN.` · then, large: `ALL SHALL BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say all shall be well. Settle, and breathe. Let one real worry come to mind, not the biggest, just a real one. Look at it honestly, the way Julian looked at her question. Don't pretend it's fine. Then, on a slow out-breath, say Julian's words quietly, or in your head: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Say them again on the next breath, and the next. If you pray, let them be your prayer. If you don't, just notice what it's like to hold a worry and a hope at the same time. The bell holds the time.
Anchoress. A woman enclosed for life in a cell beside a church, given to prayer, with one window toward the altar and one toward the town. Today's word.
Your line: all shall be well. Today, when the worry comes back, don't argue with it. Say Julian's line once, slowly, and then do the next small thing in front of you. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics read Julian's Revelations of Divine Love in prayer groups and on retreat, and some visit her rebuilt cell at Saint Julian's Church in Norwich; she is honored as Blessed or as a saint in different calendars, though she has not been formally canonized.
